{"kind":"proof","text":"Let \(n\) be a positive integer. We will prove the claim with \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=5\).

For the lower bound, suppose a terminal configuration has used \(m\) blocks. For \(n\ge2\), the board contains
\[
2n(n-2)
\]
potential triples: \(n(n-2)\) horizontal and the same number vertical. Since the configuration is terminal, every potential triple contains a removed stamp.

A horizontal removed block meets at most five horizontal potential triples: their starting positions can range only from two places before the block to two places after its beginning. Each of its three stamps belongs to at most three vertical potential triples, giving at most nine vertical triples. Thus one block meets at most \(5+9=14\) potential triples. The same holds for a vertical block. Therefore
\[
14m\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so every terminal configuration satisfies
\[
m\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
Consequently
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For \(n=1\), this inequality is immediate because its right-hand side is negative.

For the upper bound, first define a periodic collection of horizontal blocks on the infinite square grid. In row \(i\), place blocks whose starting columns are all integers congruent to \(i\pmod 5\). Thus the removed positions in row \(i\) are precisely those \((i,j)\) for which
\[
j-i\pmod5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
These blocks are pairwise disjoint, since consecutive blocks in a row have starting columns differing by five.

Every horizontal triple meets this infinite pattern, because in each row only two consecutive residue classes modulo five are unmarked. Every vertical triple also meets it: for a triple in column \(j\) and rows \(r,r+1,r+2\), the possible marked conditions are
\[
j-r\in\{0,1,2\},\qquad j-r\in\{1,2,3\},\qquad j-r\in\{2,3,4\}\pmod5,
\]
and these three sets cover all residues modulo five.

Now restrict to the \(n\times n\) board and initially tear out every one of these periodic blocks that lies wholly inside the board. In each row there are at most \(n/5+1\) such blocks, so their total number is at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n.
\]
The only marked stamps of the infinite pattern whose blocks were omitted are in the first two or last two columns: a length-three horizontal block that intersects but is not contained in the board can enter the board by at most two columns. Let \(B\) be the union of these boundary columns; then \(|B|\le4n\).

Any triple still present after the initial removals must meet \(B\), since it met a marked stamp in the infinite pattern, and that marked stamp must belong to an omitted boundary-crossing block. Continue greedily tearing out available triples until none remains. Every additional block was already available immediately after the initial removals, hence meets \(B\). Since the additional blocks are disjoint, there can be at most \(|B|\le4n\) of them.

We have therefore produced a terminal configuration using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Hence
\[
b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n.
\]
Combining the bounds gives, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac17n^2-\frac27n\le b(n)\le\frac15n^2+5n.
\]
Thus the required real constants may be chosen as \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=5\).","reason":"The proposed 5-by-5 construction is invalid because two listed blocks overlap and the asserted coverage fails. The periodic diagonal-shifted horizontal-block construction above repairs the upper bound."}

{"problem": {"theorem": "I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "proof_text": "Proof.  We think of the final “blocked’’ configuration as the result of tearing out \(b(n)\) disjoint 3-stamp blocks (each block either 3 in a row or 3 in a column) so that no further 3-stamp block remains.  Call any three consecutive positions in a row or in a column a “potential triple.’’  There are in all  
\[
H \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{horizontal triples,}
\qquad
V \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{vertical triples,}
\]
and hence 
\[
T \;=\;H+V \;=\;2\,n\,(n-2)
\]
potential triples that must each be “hit’’ (i.e.\ each must lose at least one stamp) by our removed blocks.

1.  Lower bound \(b(n)\ge \tfrac1{7}n^2-cn\).  
 
Fix any one of the \(b(n)\) removed blocks.  If it is a horizontal block occupying cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\), then it “hits’’ (i.e.\ destroys at least one cell of) at most
  •  all horizontal triples that include one of those three cells;  in a row of length \(n\), each interior cell lies in 3 horizontal triples and each end‐cell in 1 or 2, and one checks easily that the three consecutive cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\) together lie in at most 5 distinct horizontal triples;  
  •  all vertical triples that include one of those three cells;  each of the three removed stamps lies in at most 3 vertical triples, so altogether at most \(3\times3=9\) vertical triples.  
Hence that one horizontal block can destroy at most \(5+9=14\) of the \(T\) potential triples.  Likewise any vertical block destroys at most \(14\) potential triples.  

Since in the final configuration every one of the \(T=2n(n-2)\) potential triples must be destroyed by at least one of the removed blocks, and since each block can destroy at most \(14\) triples, we get the inequality
\[
14\,b(n)\;\ge\;2\,n(n-2)\;=\;2n^2-4n,
\]
i.e.
\[
b(n)\;\ge\;\frac{2n^2-4n}{14}
\;=\;\frac1{7}\,n^2-\frac{2}{7}\,n.
\]
Thus the stated lower bound holds with \(c=\tfrac{2}{7}\).

2.  Upper bound \(b(n)\le \tfrac1{5}n^2+dn\).

We give an explicit “tiling’’ construction with density \(1/5\), up to an \(O(n)\) boundary correction.  Assume for simplicity that \(n\) is a multiple of 5; the leftover strip of width \(<5\) on the right and top can then be handled by at most \(O(n)\) extra blocks without changing the leading term.

Partition the \(n\times n\) grid into \(\tfrac n5\times\tfrac n5\) little \(5\times5\) macrosquares.  In each \(5\times5\) macro with local coordinates \((r,c)\), \(1\le r,c\le5\), remove exactly the following 5 blocks (each of size 3):

  A)  A horizontal block in row \(r=2\), columns \(c=1,2,3\).

  B)  A horizontal block in row \(r=4\), columns \(c=3,4,5\).

  C)  A vertical block in column \(c=2\), rows \(r=3,4,5\).

  D)  A vertical block in column \(c=4\), rows \(r=1,2,3\).

  E)  A horizontal block in row \(r=5\), columns \(c=2,3,4\).

One checks by an easy (though a bit tedious) case‐by‐case verification that in this repeated pattern every horizontal triple of three consecutive stamps in any row will contain at least one removed stamp (from one of the above horizontal blocks in its macro or in an adjacent macro), and similarly every vertical triple of three consecutive stamps in any column meets one of the vertical blocks C) or D).  Thus after tearing out these \(5\) blocks in each \(5\times5\) cell there is no triple left anywhere in the \(n\times n\) square.

Since there are \(\tfrac n5\) macros in each direction, the total number of blocks used is
\[
5\;\times\;\Bigl(\frac n5\Bigr)^2
\;=\;\frac15\,n^2.
\]
Adding the \(O(n)\) extra blocks needed to cover the final partial strips (of width \(<5\)) along the top and right edges gives
\[
b(n)\;\le\;\frac15\,n^2 \;+\;O(n).
\]
Hence the upper bound holds with some constant \(d\).

Combining (1) and (2) completes the proof: for all \(n>0\),
\[
\frac1{7}\,n^2-\frac{2}{7}n\;\le\;b(n)\;\le\;\frac1{5}\,n^2+d\,n,
\]
as required.  ∎", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "rule_candidates": [{"id": "grp_normal_quotient", "name": "Quotient group criterion", "statement": "If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.", "conditions": ["N is a subgroup of G", "N is normal in G"], "conclusion": "G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.", "rule_digest": "f6d458aa2e7463efeea7a535cdbe0f0f7930259cfe7f845b5350ec03454da876", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "ring_quotient_ideal", "name": "Quotient ring criterion", "statement": "If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.", "conditions": ["I is a two-sided ideal of R"], "conclusion": "R/I is a ring and coset operations are well-defined.", "rule_digest": "5c419f063bbc02eba57c0943d5ecce5f2e4c1b370cbb5ad6d69c2e08c3b21835", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "grp_first_iso", "name": "First isomorphism theorem for groups", "statement": "If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "conditions": ["phi is a group homomorphism", "ker(phi) is the kernel of phi"], "conclusion": "G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "rule_digest": "335c687d26f64e41584f1b8bc575aec9d78223b01c4821bf0056bf8533de0c19", "applicability": "unchecked"}]}
